![high](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/high-priority.svg)

This script installs development packages for GTK4 (`libgtk-4-dev`, `libgdk-4-dev`). However, the project has been migrated from GTK4 to GTK3. This script will install the wrong libraries, causing the build to fail. It should be updated to install the correct GTK3 development packages (e.g., `libgtk-3-dev`).

```suggestion
sudo apt install -y \
    libgtk-3-dev    \
    libgdk-pixbuf-2.0-dev    \
    libcairo2-dev   \
    libpango1.0-dev
```

![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

The version has been downgraded from `0.2.0` to `0.1.0`. While this is acceptable for a complete rewrite, it's an unusual practice. Typically, major refactors or rewrites that change the public API or core functionality would be a major version bump (e.g., to `1.0.0` or `0.2.0` if still in pre-release). Downgrading can be confusing for users and downstream consumers. Consider adhering to Semantic Versioning for future changes.

Using `sudo` directly within a build script can be problematic for security and automation. It assumes the user running the script has `sudo` privileges and is willing to grant them without a prompt. This can fail in CI/CD environments or surprise users. It's better practice to document the required system dependencies in the `README.md` and instruct the user to install them manually.

body:
![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

Using a fixed `thread::sleep` to wait for the window to hide before taking a screenshot is brittle. The required delay can vary depending on system load and the window manager's performance. This can lead to race conditions where the screenshot is taken too early (capturing the application window) or the delay is unnecessarily long. While finding a perfectly synchronized method can be difficult, this approach is unreliable and should be considered a temporary workaround.

![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

The raw image data from `capture_x11` is processed multiple times for different purposes (saving a debug image, base64 encoding, and creating a pixbuf). This involves redundant BGRA-to-RGB/RGBA conversions, which is inefficient.

A better approach would be to perform the BGRA-to-RGBA conversion once, create an `image::RgbaImage`, and then reuse this image object for all subsequent operations. This would centralize the conversion logic, improve performance, and make the code easier to understand.

![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

Parsing the API response by chaining `[]` operators and `.unwrap_or()` is fragile and can lead to unexpected behavior or panics if the JSON structure changes. It's more robust to define structs that mirror the expected JSON response and use `serde_json::from_value` or `response.json()` to deserialize the response into these structs. This provides type safety and better error handling.

![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

This prototype, `jp_ocr_app`, appears to be a direct copy of the main `lenzu` application. This introduces significant code duplication, making the project harder to maintain. It would be better to either develop new features within the main `lenzu` crate (perhaps under a feature flag) or ensure the prototype is functionally distinct and is eventually merged or removed, rather than maintaining a parallel copy.

body:
![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

The object detection post-processing logic is very basic. It finds only the single detection with the highest confidence score across all classes. A typical object detection pipeline should:
1. Apply a confidence threshold to filter out low-confidence detections.
2. Perform Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS) for each class to merge overlapping bounding boxes for the same object.
3. Handle multiple object detections, not just the single best one.

While this might be sufficient for a simple prototype, it won't work well in real-world scenarios with multiple or overlapping objects.

Clamping `win_x`/`win_y` to 0 will break capture positioning on multi-monitor setups where the cursor can have negative coordinates (monitors left/above the primary). It’d be better to keep signed coordinates end-to-end (and handle X11 `i16` bounds explicitly) rather than silently shifting the capture region.
```suggestion
                    win_x,
                    win_y,
```

This setup script doesn’t use `set -e` (or similar) and will continue after failed `apt` commands, potentially leaving a partially configured environment. Consider adding strict-mode (`set -euo pipefail`) and/or explicit error checks so failures are surfaced early.

body:
Commenting out the Windows OCR module here effectively removes Windows Media OCR support at the module level. If the intent is to keep Windows support but avoid non-Windows builds, prefer using `#[cfg(target_os = "windows")]` on the module rather than leaving commented-out code that can drift out of date.
```suggestion
#[cfg(target_os = "windows")]
pub mod ocr_winmedia;
```

`gtk` v0.18 is GTK3, but `connect_key_press_event` expects an `Inhibit` return value. Returning `glib::Propagation::Proceed` here will not type-check; switch to returning `gtk::Inhibit(false)` (or `true` to stop propagation).
```suggestion
        gtk::Inhibit(false)
```

Similarly, commenting out the WinAPI capture module makes Windows builds silently lose functionality and leaves dead code behind. Prefer a `#[cfg(...)] pub mod capture_winapi;` gate (and keep the file compiling under that gate) rather than commenting the module out entirely.
```suggestion
#[cfg(all(target_os = "windows", feature = "gtk"))]
pub mod capture_winapi;
```

This file uses the GTK3 `gtk` crate but returns `glib::Propagation` from signal handlers (`connect_key_press_event`/`connect_draw`). In GTK3 those handlers return `gtk::Inhibit`, so this won’t compile as-is; update the handlers to return `gtk::Inhibit(false)` (or `true` to stop propagation).
```suggestion
        gtk::Inhibit(false)
```

`call_api` doesn’t validate the HTTP status code or set a timeout; failures will likely surface as empty strings rather than actionable errors. Add a request timeout and check `res.status()` before attempting to parse JSON so API/credential issues are reported clearly.

`std::thread::sleep` is called inside the 16ms polling timeout, which blocks the GTK main loop and will make the UI stutter/freeze during captures. Consider driving capture via non-blocking `glib` timeouts (or moving capture off-thread) instead of sleeping in the callback.

`connect_draw` in GTK3 expects the handler to return `gtk::Inhibit`, but this closure returns `glib::Propagation::Proceed`. This should be updated to return `gtk::Inhibit(false)` so the file compiles with the `gtk` crate.
```suggestion
        gtk::Inhibit(false)
```

`scripts/setup.sh` installs GTK4 development packages, but the main `lenzu` crate now depends on GTK3 (`gtk = "0.18"`). Either update the script to install the GTK3 packages needed by the current code, or keep the code on GTK4 to match the setup instructions.

body: `call_api` does not check `res.status()` or handle non-2xx responses, and it has no request timeout—both can lead to confusing empty results or hangs. Consider adding a client timeout, failing fast on non-success status codes (reading the error body), and returning a structured error when the expected JSON fields are missing.
